sector: Discrete manufacturing (generic OEM with upstream supplier and downstream customer; no named case)
hitl_conditions: Manual rescheduling by a supervisor/operator stays viable only for simple plans with loose timing; complex, tightly coupled schedules require system recalculation; rare exogenous risks (strikes, severe weather) enter as a manager-set input parameter.
key_finding: Conceptual three-module framework: ML supplier-risk prediction (RF/SVM/kNN/ANN) feeds a shop-floor digital twin whose sense-and-respond ML model recommends rescheduling; the twin simulates and validates the schedule before it is pushed to MES for execution; a transit module cascades delays to customer delivery dates. No implementation or results.
citation_locator: Text read = HAL author manuscript hal-04030352 (CC BY 4.0); Springer version of record via Hull proxy showed 'This is a preview of subscription content'. HAL PDF page n = paper page n-2 (published pp. 218-227). Key finding: Abstract (PDF p.3); Sec. 3 Machine Learning-Enabled Digital Twin Framework, Fig. 2 three modules (PDF pp.6-7, paper pp.4-5); Sec. 4.2 Digital Twin Learning Engine (PDF pp.8-10, paper pp.6-8); Sec. 5 Conclusions (PDF p.11, paper p.9). Twin: Sec. 2.2 (PDF p.5); Sec. 4.2 DT mirrors shop floor with ERP/APS/MES data, Fig. 3 physical factory / digital factory / mapping (PDF p.9); shared database, automated services, DT simulation validates the recommended schedule, then manufacturing management systems updated for execution (PDF p.10). AI: Sec. 4.1 Supplier Risk Prediction Module, RF/SVM/kNN/ANN/logistic regression, classification (days-late) or regression (arrival date) (PDF pp.7-8); Sec. 4.2 Sense-and-Respond ML Model trained with SVM/AdaBoost/RF/ANN (PDF p.10); Sec. 4.3 Customer Transit Module, ensemble of classifiers per transport mode, 'machine learning or optimization' (PDF p.10). HITL: Sec. 1 ML within the twin replaces offline adjustments / expert knowledge (PDF p.4); Sec. 4.1 environmental-risk input parameter 'as determined by the supply chain manager' (PDF p.8); Sec. 4.2 manual rescheduling by supervisor/operator described as current policy, feasible only if the plan is not too complex and timing not too tight, quality depends on the supervisor's prediction (PDF pp.8-9); model outputs shown on dashboards 'for human consumption' (PDF p.10); Sec. 4.3 baseline transit time 'established by the shipment planner' (PDF p.10). No human approval step is described in the recommend-validate-execute loop.

quotes.text: The Digital Twin Learning Engine is comprised of two parts, the Digital Twin and the Sense-and-Respond Machine Learning Model. The Digital Twin mirrors real-world operations on the shop floor

quotes.text: In this way, disruptions along the supply chain from supplier to manufacturing through delivery to the end customer are cascaded and incorporated into projected delivery date.
quotes.section: 4.3 Customer Transit Module (HAL PDF p.10, paper p.8)

quotes.text: A number of machine learning methods will be explored including random forest, support vector machines, k-nearest neighbors and ANNs, or logistic regression for binary target outputs.
quotes.section: 4.1 Supplier Risk Prediction Model (HAL PDF p.8, paper p.6)

quotes.text: By implementing machine learning within a digital twin framework, it is possible to continuously update the model with real-time data instead of relying on offline adjustments to the production schedule or expert knowledge.
Once validated, this information is then updated in the manufacturing management systems for execution of the revised schedule on the factory floor.

quotes.text: Model outputs are consumed by another auxiliary service/software application that will store the result(s) in the shared database and can also transform the outputs into visualizations for human consumption and display on pre-programmed dashboards.
